passage:
Zainab,
I'm writing this because saying it in the canteen felt wrong.
For about a month you've told me you already ate at home, but your tiffin comes back full, and you've started eating alone in the library. Every time we meet you ask which clothes make you look smaller, and you talk about shape more than about cricket, which you used to love.
I'm not going to say anything about how you look. That isn't the point. The point is that I miss you and I'm worried.
I won't nag you to eat either. But I think a doctor should know what's going on. Would you talk to your Ammi, or come with me to the school nurse on Monday? I'll wait outside.
You can be angry with me. I'm still your friend.
Abhinav

qa.q: Where has Zainab started eating?
qa.a: Alone in the library.

qa.q: What is Abhinav worried about, and what shows it?
qa.a: Abhinav is worried about Zainab's health; the letter lists a full tiffin, eating alone and constant talk of shape, and says "I miss you and I'm worried."

qa.q: Which choice in the letter keeps it caring rather than blaming?
qa.a: Abhinav chose not to comment on Zainab's looks or nag about eating, and instead offered to go with Zainab to the school nurse.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel reading "You can be angry with me. I'm still your friend"?
qa.a: Zainab might feel caught out at first, but also safe that the friendship will survive the honesty.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing skipped meals, eating alone and constant talk about shape, and expressing care without body comments or forcing food while pointing toward medical help.

passage: When the group leader asked me to share tonight, I almost said no. I'm Binita, Jaya's mother. Last winter Jaya, who is fifteen, started saying she'd eaten at a friend's house. Then I found her lunch wrapped in paper at the bottom of her schoolbag. She began taking her plate to her room. And every conversation turned to her waist, her arms, who looked thin. My first move was wrong. I put a full plate in front of her and said, "You'll sit until it's finished." She cried and locked her door. That night I knocked and said only, "I love you. I'm not angry. I'm scared, and I think we need the doctor's help." I didn't say one word about her body. Next morning we went to our family doctor together, and he sent us to a specialist. It's slow. But she talks to me again.

qa.q: Where did Binita find Jaya's lunch?
qa.a: Wrapped in paper at the bottom of her schoolbag.

qa.q: How did Jaya likely feel when told to sit until the plate was finished?
qa.a: Jaya likely felt forced and ashamed, which is why she cried and locked her door.

qa.q: What changed between Binita's first move and the talk that night?
qa.a: Binita dropped the forcing, said she loved Jaya and was scared, avoided any comment on her body, and took her to the family doctor next morning.

qa.q: What would change for Jaya if Binita had kept insisting on the full plate?
qa.a: Jaya might have hidden food even more and stopped talking to her mother, making help harder to reach.

grounding: It shows a mother who notices hidden lunches, secrecy and talk about shape, drops forcing food and instead expresses care and seeks medical support.

passage: I'm Samir, Pallavi's older brother. I can't know what's going on in her head, but I've noticed things. For weeks she's said "I already ate at tuition" almost every evening. I found food wrapped in tissue in her school bag. And all she talks about is her shape, which jeans look wrong, whose arms are thinner. I wanted to shout, "Just eat something!" I didn't. One night I knocked and said, "Pallu, I love you. I've noticed you're skipping meals and it worries me." I didn't say a word about how she looks. She cried and said I didn't understand. That night I told our parents what I'd seen. On Saturday Mummy took her to the doctor, and I went too.

qa.q: What did Samir find in Pallavi's school bag?
qa.a: He found food wrapped in tissue.

qa.q: How did Samir feel about what he noticed?
qa.a: He felt worried and tempted to shout at her to eat, but he held back out of care.

qa.q: What did Samir do that was wise?
qa.a: He expressed love and concern without commenting on her body or forcing food, told their parents and supported the doctor visit.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Samir said he was worried?
qa.a: She may have felt exposed and defensive, which is why she cried and said he didn't understand.

grounding: Shows a brother noticing skipped meals, secrecy around food and constant talk of shape, expressing care without commenting on the body and encouraging medical help.

passage:
Monday: Vinita noticed her daughter Bidisha, fifteen, skip breakfast again. "I'll eat at school, Ma." At dinner, she said she'd eaten at a friend's.
Thursday: Vinita found a bag of untouched lunches hidden behind Bidisha's cupboard. Bidisha kept asking, "Do my legs look big in this?" Vinita's first urge was to say, "You're too thin, sit down and eat!" She stopped herself.
Saturday: Vinita sat on Bidisha's bed. "I love you. I've noticed you're skipping meals, and I'm worried. I'm not angry. I won't talk about your body. But I want us to see Dr Mehta together." Bidisha went stiff, then whispered, "Okay." Vinita booked the appointment for Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Vinita find behind Bidisha's cupboard?
qa.a: She found a bag of untouched lunches.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when Bidisha asked about her legs?
qa.a: She wanted to say Bidisha was too thin and make her eat, a worried, frightened reaction she chose not to act on.

qa.q: How did Vinita approach Bidisha wisely on Saturday?
qa.a: She expressed love and worry, said she wasn't angry, avoided comments about the body and suggested seeing the doctor together.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when her mother said she wouldn't talk about her body?
qa.a: She may have felt less judged and safer, which is why she whispered "Okay" after going stiff.

grounding: Shows a mother noticing skipped meals, secrecy about food and talk about shape, expressing care without body comments or forcing food, and arranging medical support.

passage: "Jomon, you're worried about your sister's meals, na? Let me tell you what I did wrong once. Years ago, my daughter Priti, sixteen, started skipping meals. Always 'ate outside.' She hid food and talked only about her waist. I panicked. I said, 'You look like a skeleton! Sit and eat!' I stood over her plate. She hid more, and stopped talking to me. Then her school counsellor told me, 'Don't talk about her body. Don't force food. Tell her you care.' So I did. I said, 'Priti, I love you. I'm worried.' And we went to a doctor together. It took a long time, but she's well now. So, Jomon, no comments on your sister's body. Tell her you care, and tell your parents." Kiran Uncle sighed.

qa.q: What did Kiran say to Priti when he panicked?
qa.a: He said, 'You look like a skeleton! Sit and eat!'

qa.q: How did young Kiran feel when Priti started skipping meals?
qa.a: He felt panicked and frightened, which led him to comment on her body and stand over her plate.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Priti?
qa.a: The counsellor's advice to stop commenting on her body or forcing food and simply say he cared, followed by seeing a doctor together.

qa.q: How might Priti have felt when her father stood over her plate?
qa.a: She likely felt watched and pressured, which made her hide more and stop talking to him.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing his daughter's skipped meals and secrecy, learning to express care without body comments or forcing food, and seeking medical help.

passage:
The school trip bus to Mahabaleshwar left at six, and there was no time for breakfast. Charu noticed that Ankita didn't touch the sandwiches either at the stop or at lunch. "Not hungry," Ankita said, again, and hid her packed lunch in her bag.
It had been like this for weeks. Ankita talked constantly about "fixing" her shape and went quiet if anyone offered food.
Charu wanted to say, "You're fine, just eat." She didn't. At the viewpoint, away from the others, she said, "I've noticed you're skipping meals a lot. I'm not judging you. I just care about you and I'm worried."
Ankita's eyes filled. "Please don't tell anyone."
"I care too much to keep it secret. Let's tell Mrs Pinto together."
That evening on the bus back, Mrs Pinto sat with Ankita and called her mother to plan a doctor's visit.

qa.q: Where did the school trip bus go?
qa.a: To Mahabaleshwar.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she chose her words at the viewpoint?
qa.a: She felt worried and caring, and careful not to judge Ankita or comment on her body.

qa.q: What did Charu do well, and why was it wiser than "just eat"?
qa.a: She spoke privately with care and concern, avoided body comments or forcing food, and brought in a trusted teacher the same day so medical support could follow.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Charu says she won't keep it secret?
qa.a: She might feel scared and exposed at first, and also a little relieved that someone noticed and cared.

grounding: Charu notices a friend's skipped meals, secrecy and talk about shape, expresses care without body comments, and brings in an adult for medical support.
